title: The man from the city's edge
hookLine: a man runs from the edge of the city to tell his people to follow the messengers (36:20–27)

cards: A town meeting has turned ugly. Messengers have come, first two, then a third to back them up, and the townspeople aren't having it. You're just bad luck, they say.
Stop, or we'll stone you. Voices are rising in the square. And then, from the far side of town, from the outskirts, someone is running.
Not walking, running. He's not a messenger. He's not a leader.
The Qur'an doesn't even give his name. He just couldn't stay home.

teach.h: FROM THE EDGE, A MAN RUNNING.
teach.b: Surah Ya-Sin, verse twenty. Pickthall: "And there came from the uttermost part of the city a man running. He cried: O my people! Follow those who have been sent!" The uttermost part of the city: the edge, far from power.
Running: he didn't wait to see how it would turn out. His first argument is simple.

teach.h: THEY ASK NO PAYMENT FROM YOU.
teach.b: Verse twenty-one: follow those who ask no payment from you, and who are rightly guided. They want nothing from you; that's how you can tell.
Then he speaks about himself: why shouldn't I worship the One who created me, to whom you'll all return? I believe in your Lord, so listen to me. The Qur'an doesn't narrate what happened next.
It cuts straight to verse twenty-six: it was said to him, enter the Garden. Many commentators understand from this that his people killed him.
And his first words in paradise are the most surprising part: if only my people knew how my Lord has forgiven me and honored me. No anger. No wish for revenge.

He still wants them to make it. A saying in the commentaries, attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, puts it this way: he gave his people good advice while he was alive, and he wished them well after they killed him.
Tradition calls him Habib the carpenter, and many place the town at Antioch, but the Qur'an names neither. He's the man from the edge, and that's enough.

how: Muslim preachers often tell the story of the man from the city's edge as an example of courage and of sincere goodwill toward people who reject you; tradition names him Habib al-Najjar.

games.q: you've been killed for defending the messengers, and you're told: enter the Garden. what's the first thing you say?
o: if only my people knew how my Lord forgave me.
games.why: he still wished his people knew. commentators say he advised them in life and wished them well after they killed him.

practice: Think of someone in your life, at work, in your family, online, who's saying something true and getting no support.
Picture yourself, like the man from the edge, walking over to stand next to them, and hear what you'd say, kept short, the way he did. Rest there a moment.

wordCard.voice: Habib, tradition's name for the man who ran from the city's edge in Surah Ya-Sin to defend the messengers, and was killed for it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a man, hurrying. yas'a is the same root as sa'y, the walk between Safa and Marwa.

carryVoice: Your line: he came running. No name in the text, only the running. See you tomorrow.
